technique: Appears to be 3D CGI rendered to emulate a stop-motion/claymation look rather than literal stop-motion: the woman's sweater has a fuzzy felt-fiber shader with individually visible fibers, the man's skin has soft subsurface-scattering shading, and the background has true lens-like bokeh (out-of-focus autumn trees) that shifts subtly between frames -- these are traits of a 3D renderer, not a physical camera on a motion-control rig. No fingerprints, tool marks, or armature dents are visible on the surfaces, which argues against handmade clay/puppet stop-motion despite the tactile felt/wool texturing. Flagging genuine uncertainty: without inter-frame video (only ~1s-spaced keyframes available) I cannot confirm whether motion is truly continuous/smooth or held on 2s/3s CG poses, but the near-identical poses across consecutive periodic frames suggest a deliberately restrained, mostly-static character rig moved in a small number of discrete held poses per line.
facial_animation_notes: Faces stay in almost the same set pose across most of the periodic frames (periodic-0 through periodic-8) despite different caption words appearing under them, suggesting mouths/jaws are barely animated for lip-sync and the joke is carried more by captions than facial performance. The one visible change is the man's eyebrows/eyelids: his lids track from a skeptical half-closed squint (periodic-0/1) to a wider, more startled look with visible eye-white by periodic-9 alongside a slightly open mouth, reading as a delayed reaction beat right before the title/credit card. The woman's face is essentially locked in a single flat, unimpressed expression (heavy-lidded eyes, downturned mouth corner) for the entire span of frames sampled.
eye_and_blink_notes: No blink is caught in any of the 12 periodic frames -- both characters keep eyes open throughout, consistent with either very infrequent blinking or blinks landing between the ~1s sampling intervals. The woman's eyes stay in a fixed heavy-lidded, slightly averted-down gaze at the man across all frames (no saccades visible). The man's eyes shift from squinting down over his glasses (periodic-0 through periodic-6) to a rounder, more open-eyed look in periodic-9, the clearest eye-acting change in the sequence.
head_movement_notes: Both heads hold essentially the same tilt and yaw for most of the runtime -- the woman's head stays angled up-and-right toward the man with no measurable turn across periodic-0 to periodic-9. The man shows a very slight downward chin dip/settle between periodic-6 ("LET") and periodic-9, and his head appears marginally tipped back by periodic-9 (mouth open, brow raised), the only clear head-pose change identified across the sampled frames. No camera movement is visible in any frame -- the wide two-shot composition (seesaw, park background, title card position) is pixel-for-pixel static throughout, indicating a locked-off single shot for the whole video.
gesture_notes: The single clear gesture in the sampled frames: the man raises both hands from the seesaw handle up to his glasses/face between periodic-3 ("ALREADY") and periodic-4 ("THAT"), then both hands are back down gripping the seesaw handle by periodic-5 ("AT") -- a fast up-and-back-down adjust-the-glasses or rub-the-face beat that reads as an exasperated reaction. The woman's hands stay clasped/resting on her side of the seesaw handle in an identical position across every single frame, showing no gestural animation at all for her character.
idle_motion_notes: Aside from the one glasses-touch gesture, both figures are otherwise held static: no visible weight shift, no seesaw tilt/bounce, no cloth or hair sway despite the fuzzy sweater and felt textures, and no secondary motion in the leaves or grass. The autumn trees in the deep background show soft continuous blur/bokeh but no discernible wind motion between frames. This produces a very "frozen tableau" idle state where the joke's comic tension comes from the characters' stillness and stare rather than fidgeting or ambient motion.
frame_rate_feel: Source is 30fps per metadata.json, but the sampled periodic frames (spaced roughly one second apart across an 11.7s clip) show almost no incremental change between most consecutive frames, implying the actual character animation is posed on far fewer keys than 30/sec -- it reads as sparse, held-pose animation (long holds punctuated by rare short gesture beats like the glasses touch) rather than continuously eased motion. The overall feel is deliberately deadpan and stiff/inert, closer to a slideshow of near-identical stills than fluid full animation, which suits the deadpan-stare comedic tone.
overall_animation_style_notes: The piece is built as a single locked-off wide shot of two seated figures on a seesaw with a shallow-depth-of-field autumn park background, bold sans-serif karaoke-style word-by-word captions burned in at the bottom, and a large serif title card ("THAT LOOK", episode number) plus an end-card ("LOW BATTERY PEOPLE / CREATED BY NIN.") composited over the same static background plate. Character design mixes a soft fuzzy-felt shader on the woman's sweater against a smooth, almost rubber/plastic finish on the man's exaggerated long nose and glossy black rounded torso (visually reading like a stylized battery/device silhouette, matching the "low battery people" title). The restrained, near-static animation combined with heavy reliance on text captions and a single sustained expression per character strongly suggests the comedy is driven by writing/timing and voice performance rather than expressive character animation -- movement is used sparingly as punctuation (one gesture, one late eye/mouth reaction) rather than continuously.
